stories.title: Medical Outpatient Building Sales Surge in H1 2026
stories.excerpt: Improving capital market conditions, expanding lender appetite and resilient operating fundamentals have driven a surge in medical outpatient building (MOB) investment sales activity, Cushman & Wakefield reported. MOB transaction volume reached $6.7 billion in the first half of 2026, a 21% increase year-over-year. MOB cap rates, meanwhile, declined 35 basis points Y-O-Y to 6.8%, while average asset pricing reached $368 per square foot in Q2 2026. Portfolio transaction activity more than doubled relative to H1 2025, exceeding $2.6 billion, as the portfolio premium widened to 100 bps over single-asset cap rates. “Cap rate compression, renewed debt market liquidity, and rising portfolio demand all point to improving investor confidence, while steady rent growth and high occupancy levels reinforce the sector’s underlying fundamentals,” said Sandy Romero, head of office & alternatives research at Cushman & Wakefield. “With capital becoming more readily available, we expect MOBs to remain well-positioned to attract institutional investment through the balance of 2026.” The post Medical Outpatient Building Sales Surge in H1 2026 appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MOB transaction volume: $6.7B in H1 2026, +21% YoY; cap rates compressed 35 bps to 6.8%
Portfolio deal activity more than doubled to $2.6B; portfolio premium widened to 100 bps over single assets
Improving debt liquidity and institutional capital appetite signal sustained MOB investor confidence through 2026
stories.summary: Medical outpatient building investment sales surged 21% year-over-year to $6.7 billion in H1 2026, with cap rates declining 35 basis points to 6.8% and average pricing reaching $368/sf in Q2. Portfolio transaction activity more than doubled to $2.6 billion, with the portfolio premium widening to 100 bps over single-asset deals. Strong fundamentals—steady rent growth and high occupancy—combined with renewed debt liquidity are expected to sustain institutional investor interest through the remainder of 2026.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. MOB is a different asset class with separate financing, tenant profiles, and capital flows. The capital liquidity described benefits all real estate, but does not directly signal demand drivers (jobs, population, rent growth) affecting apartment markets.

stories.title: Genentech Tops Out $2B Holly Springs Manufacturing Facility
stories.excerpt: Genentech raised the final beam of its new manufacturing facility in Holly Springs, North Carolina, during a topping-out ceremony. The milestone reflects continued progress on Genentech’s approximately $2 billion investment in its first-ever East Coast manufacturing facility. The project, announced in May of 2025, broke ground in August of 2025. Completion is expected in 2029. Once operational, the 700,000-square-foot facility will produce next-generation treatments for metabolic conditions, such as obesity. It will incorporate advanced biomanufacturing, automation, robotics and the latest digital manufacturing technologies designed to increase production efficiency, support sustainability, and strengthen Genentech’s U.S.-based supply chain. The project is expected to support more than 2,000 jobs, including more than 500 high-wage manufacturing roles and more than 1,500 construction jobs. The facility is part of Roche and Genentech’s broader $50 billion commitment to R&D and manufacturing infrastructure in the U.S. Roche and Genentech’s current U.S. footprint includes 13 manufacturing sites, 15 research and development sites and approximately 25,000 employees across 24 locations in eight states. The post Genentech Tops Out $2B Holly Springs Manufacturing Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Genentech topping out $2B manufacturing facility in Holly Springs, NC; completion 2029, 700k sf
Project expected to generate 2,000+ jobs: 500 high-wage manufacturing, 1,500 construction; supports Roche's $50B US infra commitment
First East Coast facility for Genentech; part of 25,000-employee US footprint across 24 locations in 8 states
stories.summary: Genentech reached topping-out on a $2 billion, 700,000-sq-ft manufacturing facility in Holly Springs, North Carolina, announced May 2025 and broken ground August 2025, with completion expected in 2029. The facility will produce next-generation obesity treatments and support more than 2,000 jobs, including 500 high-wage manufacturing roles and 1,500 construction jobs. This is Genentech's first East Coast manufacturing site and part of Roche's broader $50 billion US R&D and manufacturing infrastructure commitment.
stories.impact: Strong demand signal for multifamily in Pasco County, NC (Holly Springs area). Influx of 500+ permanent high-wage biotech workers plus multi-year construction workforce will drive near-term and sustained rental demand; developers should underwrite apartments in accessible submarkets now—cap rates will compress and land will appreciate as job visibility increases. Window to acquire/entitle before 2028–2029 occupancy draws institutional capital to the market.

stories.title: Shifting Fortunes for L.A.’s Ports Boost Surrounding Industrial Real Estate
stories.excerpt: Ports are meant to offer protection from storms or rough seas. But nothing has been able to protect the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from the uncertainty and fluctuation of trade policy during President Donald Trump’s second term. “It’s like the quote from ‘The Morning Show,’” said Gregg Healy, executive vice president and head of Savills Industrial Services. “Chaos is the new cocaine. I do think we will have more turbulent times ahead.” So it’s been a welcome surprise that the tariff turbulence has seemed to benefit industrial real estate near or tied to the waterfront. From Liberation Day in April 2025, when Trump announced his first round of sweeping tariffs, to the current war with Iran, the ebbs and flows of global trade have been massive and disruptive, but new shipping volume is helping port-adjacent and port-dependent submarkets. Amid a boom and bust cycle that’s dominated the last few years, and pushing warehouse vacancy to a recent peak of 7 percent this year, Los Angeles’ industrial side may be poised for an upswing. People watch as a container ship departs from the Port of Los Angeles. PHOTO: Mario Tama/Getty Images Shipping volume at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach is up 1.8 percent this year. After topping 1 million container units in June, the Port of Los Angeles nearly hit that mark in July, making it the second-busiest July on record. “Businesses continue to move cargo when they see windows of opportunity amid an evolving trade environment, while resilient consumer demand is helping keep imports at historically strong levels,” said Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka in a recent statement. The region’s industrial market saw its highest leasing levels in five years during the second quarter of 2026, according to Cushman & Wakefield data, driven by its centrality to larger logistics networks. bullets: LA/Long Beach ports seeing shipping volume recovery amid Trump tariff volatility and geopolitical swings
Industrial warehouse vacancy peaked at 7% in 2026; port-adjacent and port-dependent submarkets benefiting from cargo throughput
Tariff turbulence creating boom-bust cycles but boosting near-term demand for port-proximate logistics and distribution real estate
stories.summary: Despite tariff uncertainty and Middle East geopolitical disruptions during Trump's second term, Los Angeles and Long Beach ports are experiencing a shipping volume uptick, benefiting port-adjacent and port-dependent industrial submarkets. LA industrial warehouse vacancy recently peaked at 7%, but port-proximate areas are seeing activity gains from the ebbs and flows of global trade routing and container volume shifts. The volatility creates headwinds but is supporting near-term demand for logistics and distribution facilities near the waterfront.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. Industrial and port activity do not directly correlate with apartment demand unless coupled with permanent job growth. However, logistics sector expansion and wage growth among distribution/warehouse workers in port-adjacent submarkets (Long Beach, Carson, Vernon) could indirectly support demand for workforce housing; developers should monitor logistics employment trends in these specific areas for downstream rental demand signals.

stories.title: West Palm Beach Developer Buys Lot, Apartments on Way
stories.excerpt: Estate Cos. bought a lot in West Palm Beach and plans to build the second phase of a two-phase apartment project. The S. Floirda Business Journal reports the company paid $13 million for a 1.19-acre lot at 411 West Railroad. The seller was Sunview Cos. Banesco USA provided an $8.45 million mortgage to the buyer. For the first phase, the 321-unit, eight-story Soleste Palm Station, just west of this site, is still under construction. For Phase II, The Estate Cos. plans to develop the new site with 310 apartments in 15 stories. For Soleste Palm Station Two, the multifamily community will include 411 parking spaces and a pool deck. Estate Companies says it identifies and coordinates investment opportunities for both private and institutional investors. It’s focus, since 2012, is on high-yielding, risk-adjusted, development and investment opportunities (land and residential projects) in the South Florida region. bullets: Estate Cos. acquired 1.19-acre lot, West Palm Beach for $13M; Banesco USA financed $8.45M
Phase II: 310 units in 15 stories at 411 W. Railroad, adjacent to Phase I's 321-unit Soleste Palm Station (still under construction)
Two-phase, 631-unit mixed-density project signals developer confidence in West Palm Beach rental demand and entitlement speed
stories.summary: Estate Cos. purchased a 1.19-acre lot in West Palm Beach for $13 million and secured $8.45 million in financing from Banesco USA for Phase II development. The new site will accommodate 310 apartments across 15 stories adjacent to the Phase I project, Soleste Palm Station (321 units, eight stories, still under construction), creating a two-phase, 631-unit community. Phase II will include 411 parking spaces and pool deck amenities.
stories.impact: Estate Cos.' rapid consecutive-phase acquisition and financing in West Palm Beach confirms sustained rental demand and developer confidence in South Florida market fundamentals. The 631-unit pipeline signals no overbuilding concerns locally; Phase II underwriting likely reflects strong pre-leasing or absorption of Phase I, suggesting rents and occupancy remain resilient. Competitive position tightens for other developers—land availability and cap rates in the submarket will compress as institutional capital chases similar West Palm Beach opportunities.

stories.title: McDowell Starts Work on Hudson Age-Restricted, Affordable Apartments
stories.excerpt: McDowell Housing Partners closed on a construction loan and started work on Ekos at Bayonet Point II, the second phase of a three-phase master-planned community that will bring 360 affordable homes to Pasco County. The $38.9 million development will add 120 age-restricted apartments at 7526 McDowell Way in Hudson, one block from HCA Florida Bayonet Point Hospital. Rents and incomes will be restricted across three tiers of Area Median Income (AMI). The development was financed with tax-exempt bonds issued by Florida Housing Finance Corporation (FHFC), 4% housing tax credits, and subordinate financing awarded by FHFC through its SAIL, ELI and HOME-ARP programs. Wells Fargo Community Lending & Investment provided equity through the purchase of the housing tax credits and placed the senior construction financing. Permanent financing will be provided by Freddie Mac and serviced by Wells Fargo Multifamily Capital. Amenities include a standalone clubhouse with a pool and covered patio, a fitness center, a computer lab, a game and crafts area, and a dog park. Ekos at Bayonet Point II is expected to be complete in spring 2028. The post McDowell Starts Work on Hudson Age-Restricted, Affordable Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: McDowell Housing Partners closed $38.9M construction loan, started Phase II: 120 age-restricted apartments in Hudson, FL (Pasco County)
Financing: FHFC tax-exempt bonds, 4% housing tax credits, SAIL/ELI/HOME-ARP, Wells Fargo equity and senior construction; Freddie Mac permanent
Ekos at Bayonet Point II part of 360-unit, three-phase master-planned community; completion spring 2028; near HCA Florida hospital
stories.summary: McDowell Housing Partners closed a $38.9 million construction loan and commenced Phase II of Ekos at Bayonet Point, a three-phase master-planned community in Hudson, Florida (Pasco County) that will deliver 120 age-restricted affordable apartments across three tiers of Area Median Income. Financing included tax-exempt bonds, 4% housing tax credits, and subordinate programs (SAIL, ELI, HOME-ARP) from FHFC, with Wells Fargo providing equity and senior construction financing and Freddie Mac committed for permanent financing. Completion is expected spring 2028.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to for-profit multifamily development, but signals robust public-sector and institutional appetite for age-restricted affordable housing in Pasco County. Proximity to HCA hospital anchors workforce housing demand; the three-phase model and broad subsidy stack indicate strong local demographics (aging population, healthcare workers, limited income) and tax-credit arbitrage opportunity. Market may be less competitive for market-rate development if affordable supply absorbs rent-restricted demand, but age-restricted niche remains underserved—opportunity for market-rate 55+ communities in adjacent Pasco submarkets.

stories.title: Retail Landlords Need to Underwrite Their Tenants’ Customer Base, Too
stories.excerpt: Landlords underwrite the retail tenant. But they almost never underwrite the tenant’s customer. They should. That gap costs landlords money, and it is fixable before a listing goes live. The standard leasing process is too reactive: Review comparable rents, post the space on Crexi and LoopNet, wait for responses, and then vet an operator’s finances. Mark Kvetkovskiy. None of that tells you whether enough of that retailer’s customers live near the space. If they do not, the risk rises of tenant failure, months of vacancy, and another round of commissions and negotiations. The better approach is to flip the process. Instead of waiting to see who shows up, start by studying who lives near the space. How do nearby households spend? Which categories over-index locally? Does the neighborhood support an everyday concept, a destination brand, or something in between? Answer those questions first, and you can define the customer already walking the neighborhood’s streets. Then, identify the brands that serve that customer and approach them directly about the vacancy. Proactive outreach can reduce days on market and the vacancy costs that come with them. Consider a hypothetical vacant restaurant at Rivington and Ludlow streets on Manhattan’s Lower East Side. I analyzed the 2026 Esri Consumer Spending Survey and Esri Market Potential data for the area within a five-minute walk. Esri’s modeled data draws on consumer surveys, demographic segmentation and household spending patterns. It is directional, not a record of observed transactions. Esri estimates that households in that walking area spend $50,243,250 annually on food and beverages away from home, or about $5,043 per household. The market-potential data then sharpens the picture. Some 20.4 percent of adults in the area visited a fine-dining restaurant in the previous six months, an index of 124, or 24 percent above the U.S. average. bullets: Article argues retail landlords underwrite tenant finances but ignore tenant customer base demographics and spending patterns
Gap in underwriting leads to tenant failure, prolonged vacancy, higher commissions and re-leasing costs
Proactive approach: map local household demographics and spending categories first, then target brands serving that customer base directly

Matching customer demand to tenant concept upfront is a fixable underwriting gap.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. This is a retail-specific underwriting discipline and does not affect apartment supply, demand, capital, or cost. Multifamily developers may benefit indirectly if ground-floor retail in mixed-use projects is underwritten more rigorously, reducing retail vacancy and improving project stabilization, but the article provides no data or market signals applicable to apartment underwriting.

stories.title: Inflation Is Down. But Consumers Aren’t Out of the Woods Yet
stories.excerpt: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 3.4% year over year in July. Meanwhile, the core CPI, which excludes food and energy costs, rose 2.5%. Both measures fell slightly month over month. They also matched market expectations and suggested that inflationary pressures could be moderating. A recent Marcus & Millichap report supported that possibility, noting that despite continued turmoil in the Middle East and its potential impact on supply chains, the latest readings could “modestly ease immediate pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.” Rent Growth Continues Muted Housing remains one of the largest contributors to the core CPI, with the Owners’ Equivalent Rent (OER) accounting for much of the metric. Also counted are apartment rents. These increased by 1.3%, compared with the 2.1% increase the year before. At the same time, real average hourly earnings declined 0.1%. This suggests that consumers’ purchasing power remains under pressure even as inflation moderates. Consumer Spending Faces Headwinds Food prices continued to climb in July, with year-over-year grocery and restaurant prices increasing by 2.7% and 3.4%, respectively. “Although this divergence may suggest consumers remain willing to spend on discretionary dining, it may also signal vulnerability if household purchasing power weakens further,” Marcus & Millichap said. Retail property fundamentals were mixed. Vacancy remains 60 basis points below its historical average, as space demand remains volatile. Net space relinquishment occurred in three of the past six quarters. The report suggested that retailers are working in a resilient consumer environment but are selective about spending. Hospitality Could Feel the Pressure Leisure spending is under pressure, too. bullets: CPI July 2026: +3.4% YoY; core CPI +2.5%; both fell slightly MoM and matched expectations
Apartment rents +1.3% YoY vs. +2.1% prior year; real average hourly earnings declined 0.1%, eroding purchasing power
Food/grocery/restaurant prices still climbing (+2.7% to +3.4% YoY); consumer resilience masks vulnerability if wage pressures persist
stories.summary: The Consumer Price Index rose 3.4% year-over-year in July 2026, with core CPI at 2.5%, both slightly down month-over-month and matching expectations. Apartment rents increased 1.3% year-over-year, a slowdown from 2.1% the prior year, while real average hourly earnings declined 0.1%, signaling continued consumer purchasing-power pressure. Food prices remained elevated, with grocery prices up 2.7% and restaurant prices up 3.4% year-over-year, suggesting consumers may be vulnerable to further shocks despite moderated overall inflation.
stories.impact: Rent-growth deceleration (1.3% vs. 2.1% YoY) suggests moderating demand or increased supply absorption in some markets—developers should monitor local rent growth rates closely. Flat/negative real wage growth is a caution flag: if food and discretionary costs remain elevated, tenant ability to absorb further rent increases weakens. Underwriting should model conservative rent-growth assumptions and prioritize markets with job/wage growth above inflation. Lower Fed-rate expectations from moderating CPI may ease construction financing and refinancing costs, improving development feasibility.

stories.title: T&E Development Buys West Chelsea Site for $34M From PPHE Hotel Group
stories.excerpt: A development site in Manhattan’s West Chelsea area previously conceived for hotel and luxury residences in 2019 by an international hospitality firm is now poised for a new residential journey. Amsterdam-based PPHE Hotel Group sold the property at 538-542 West 29th Street to Brooklyn-based T&E Development for $33.5 million in a deal that closed late Thursday afternoon, Commercial Observer has learned. Colliers represented the seller with a team led by Zach Redding, Dylan Kane and Jared King. Sporn Group’s Lenny Sporn arranged the sale on behalf of the buyer. Crain’s New York Business first reported that the deal was set to close this summer. PPHE Hotel Group announced in March 2019 it had formed a joint venture with developer Largo to acquire the vacant lot for around $42 million, with plans to build a 98-key hotel and 55 condos. An entity connected to PPHE field demolition permits for the project in late 2023, Crain’s reported at the time. Greg Hegarty, co-CEO of PPHE, said in a February statement on the pending sale that “significant changes to the regulatory landscape” for ground-up development of hotel projects in New York following its 2019 acquisition contributed to the decision to part ways with the property. The 9,875-square-foot vacant lot between 10th and 11th avenues has 74,063 square feet of development potential under New York City’s C6-3 zoning within the Special West Chelsea District and will not require an affordable housing component, according to Colliers. T&E recently completed a 54-unit condo development called the Florian at 350 East 18th Street in Manhattan’s Gramercy Park. Redding said the property is one of the few remaining unconstrained development sites in West Chelsea and would be well positioned as a residential project given there is only one condo building currently under construction between West 20th and West 30th streets. He noted that nearby condo developments have netted average sales of roughly $2,884 per square fo
bullets: T&E Development acquired West Chelsea development site, Manhattan (538-542 W. 29th St.) from PPHE Hotel Group for $33.5M
PPHE paid ~$42M in 2019 JV with Largo for hotel/condo concept (98 keys, 55 condos); now pivoting to residential
Asset repricing from hospitality to residential signals hotel-to-multifamily conversion thesis; West Chelsea market favors apartments over hotels post-pandemic
stories.summary: T&E Development purchased a Manhattan West Chelsea development site (538-542 West 29th Street) from Amsterdam-based PPHE Hotel Group for $33.5 million. PPHE had acquired the vacant lot in a 2019 joint venture with developer Largo for approximately $42 million, planning a 98-key hotel with 55 condominiums; the project was abandoned after late-2023 demolition permits were filed. T&E's acquisition signals a shift to residential-focused development in the Manhattan submarket.
stories.impact: Significant signal for Manhattan multifamily. Hotel-to-residential conversion thesis strengthens: PPHE's loss on the 2019 deal (paid ~$42M, sold at $33.5M) reflects sustained weakness in Manhattan hospitality development and rising relative value of residential. West Chelsea's proximity to Hudson Yards, high foot traffic, and transit access make it attractive for rentals rather than hotel keys or condos in current cycle. Developers should eye other Manhattan hotel sites and underperforming hotel assets for conversion or repurposing; cap rates and land costs may still be compressed vs. pre-pandemic, but conversion economics are improving as multifamily demand stabilizes and hotel capex burden deters new hotel development.

stories.title: L.A. County Investment Sales Jump 28% in July Thanks to Multifamily
stories.excerpt: Commercial real estate investment sales accelerated across Los Angeles County in July, with multifamily accounting for the majority of capital deployed. About 7.25 million square feet of commercial property traded for $2.1 billion last month, NAI Capital reported Thursday, citing CoStar data. Compared to July 2025, almost 22 percent more square footage traded hands during July to make for a 28.5 percent jump in dollar volume. Compared with July 2024, sales volume climbed 75 percent. The gains came despite elevated borrowing costs, with long-term Treasury yields remaining near multiyear highs. Multifamily dominated, with 3.43 million square feet changing hands for $1.22 billion — accounting for 58 percent of all investment during the month in L.A. County. Sales volume increased 55 percent since last year, and almost 166 percent compared to July 2024. Average pricing rose 28.7 percent to $376 per square foot. People look at the Los Angeles skyline from Griffith Observatory. PHOTO: Matt McNulty - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images Retail also posted broad gains. About 1.23 million square feet sold for $402 million, pushing dollar volume up 40 percent from a year ago, and nearly doubling the July 2024 total. Retail square footage traded has climbed 135 percent over the same two-year period. Industrial faces a more complicated environment. About 1.33 million square feet traded in July, which is almost 71 percent higher since 2025, but dollar volume remained about flat at $214 million, and average pricing fell 3.6 percent to $273 per square foot. Office was the only major property type to decline in both sales volume and square footage. About 1.26 million square feet sold for $262 million, down 9.7 percent and 23.4 percent, respectively, from July 2025. Average pricing dropped 23.5 percent to $250 per square foot. Compared with July 2024, the amount of office space traded has fallen by roughly half. “As we head into the fall, the key question is not simply whether investment acti
bullets: LA County investment sales: $2.1B (7.25M sf) in July 2026, +28.5% YoY, +75% vs. July 2024
Multifamily dominated: $1.22B (3.43M sf, 58% of county volume); +55% YoY, +166% vs. July 2024; avg. price $376/sf (+28.7%)
Elevated Treasury yields despite strong sales volume signal active investor appetite overriding borrowing-cost headwinds
stories.summary: Los Angeles County commercial real estate investment sales jumped to $2.1 billion (7.25 million sq ft) in July 2026, up 28.5% year-over-year and 75% compared to July 2024. Multifamily led the charge with $1.22 billion in transactions (3.43 million sq ft, 58% of county volume), up 55% year-over-year and 166% versus July 2024, with average pricing rising 28.7% to $376 per square foot. The surge occurred despite elevated long-term Treasury yields remaining near multiyear highs.
stories.impact: Strong confirmation that LA multifamily capital markets are heating fast—July 2026 multifamily volume up 166% in two years signals major institutional capital inflow and reduced distress selling. Price appreciation (+28.7% YoY per sf) and transaction velocity suggest cap rates have likely compressed further; developers must move quickly on LA-area land acquisitions and development approvals before values spike higher. Paradoxically, elevated Treasury yields typically depress cap-rate compression, yet sales volume surged—indicates supply scarcity and income-growth confidence overwhelming rate headwinds. Window to finance new development may be tightening; lock in construction debt and mezzanine capital now.

stories.title: New York City’s Technology Labor Market Has Surpassed San Francisco: Report
stories.excerpt: It’s official. New York is employing more tech workers than the San Francisco Bay area. According to an annual CBRE report on North American tech talent, the New York metropolitan area’s tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025. The stat marks an 8.4 percent increase from 2022 that added 30,640 jobs. Meanwhile, San Francisco’s tech employment fell by 6 percent over the same period, totaling 375,730 jobs in 2025. This is the first time in the report’s 13-year history that the Big Apple has come out ahead. The city’s diversified job market helped set it apart, Colin Yasukochi, executive director of CBRE’s tech insights center, told Commercial Observer. “What really pushed New York past the San Francisco Bay Area has been the job reductions that we’ve seen [in San Francisco], with a lot of the announced layoffs, and the fact that New York has continued to grow,” Yasukochi said. San Francisco remains in North America’s top spot for its pool of tech talent, however, ranked across 13 metrics. The report, which analyzed the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and LinkedIn data, found that tech jobs make up more than 10 percent of total employment in San Francisco, compared to just 4.2 percent in New York. But a whopping 61 percent of San Francisco’s tech talent works directly in the tech industry, according to CBRE’s report, leaving its general labor market vulnerable. In New York City, just 34 percent of its tech workers work within the industry, while 21 percent work in tech roles in finance, insurance and real estate industries (otherwise known as FIRE). “[That] has given New York resilience from the tech downturn that broadly started in 2022, in terms of employment,” Yasukochi said. “But, obviously, with the artificial intelligence industry coming into play, that’s turned around quite substantially in the last year.” Yasukochi added that New York also benefits from a massive university infrastructure and lower wages than San Francisco, on average, for
bullets: NYC metro tech employment: 394,300 in 2025, +8.4% vs. 2022 (+30,640 jobs); surpassed SF Bay Area (375,730, -6% vs. 2022)
First time in CBRE's 13-year report history that NYC tops SF; SF job losses from announced layoffs vs. NYC diversified growth
NYC remains #2 for overall tech talent pool quality across 13 metrics; diversification (non-tech jobs) drove NY's competitive advantage
stories.summary: New York City's metropolitan area tech workforce reached 394,300 in 2025, a gain of 30,640 jobs (+8.4%) since 2022 and surpassing the San Francisco Bay Area's 375,730 tech workers (down 6% over the same period). This is the first time in CBRE's 13-year annual report history that NYC has led. NYC's diversified job market and continued growth, contrasted with San Francisco's announced tech layoffs, drove the crossover. San Francisco remains ranked #2 in overall tech talent pool quality across 13 metrics.
stories.impact: Major demand catalyst for NYC multifamily, especially in Manhattan core and outer-borough tech hubs (Brooklyn, Long Island City). 30,640 net tech jobs added since 2022 represent high-wage in-migration; developers should underwrite luxury and upper-mid-market rental demand in proximity to major tech clusters (Flatiron, Hudson Yards, SoHo, Brooklyn Tech Triangle). Conversely, SF Bay Area weakness signals potential weakening rental demand in San Francisco and adjacent markets—exercise caution on new Bay Area starts unless tied to specific growth corridors. NYC's diversification advantage suggests resilience in rents even if tech growth moderates; mixed-income underwriting in secondary NYC markets may outperform single-industry-dependent SF submarkets.
